The following day he stayed inside the house, spending most of it in his own room. He was sick with a frantic fear of death, yet felt no interest in living. The feeling that he was being hunted, trapped, and followed had begun to take over his mind. If a tapestry merely stirred in the breeze, he trembled. The dead leaves blowing against the leaded windows seemed like his own broken promises and desperate regrets. Whenever he shut his eyes, he saw the sailor’s face again, peering through the misty glass, and felt horror grip his heart once more.

But perhaps his imagination alone had summoned revenge from the darkness and placed those dreadful visions of punishment before him. Real life was a confusion of events, while the imagination followed a terrifying logic. It was imagination that made regret follow closely behind wrongdoing. Imagination made every crime give birth to its own twisted offspring. In the everyday world of facts, the wicked went unpunished and the good went unrewarded. The strong were granted success, and the weak were forced to fail. That was all. Besides, if a stranger had been lurking around the house, the servants or gamekeepers would have noticed him. If there had been footprints in the flower beds, the gardeners would have reported them. Yes, it had only been his imagination. Sibyl Vane’s brother had not returned to murder him. He had sailed away in his ship to sink in some winter sea. He was safe from that man, at least. Why, the man did not know who he was, could not possibly know. His youthful appearance had protected him.

And yet, if it had all been an illusion, how dreadful to think that his conscience could create such terrifying ghosts, give them visible bodies, and make them move in front of him! What would his life become if, night and day, the shadows of his crime stared from quiet corners, mocked him from hiding places, whispered in his ear while he sat at dinner, and woke him with freezing fingers while he slept? As this thought passed through his mind, his face turned pale with fear, and the air seemed suddenly colder. Oh, what a frenzy of madness had driven him to kill his friend! Even the memory of that scene was unbearable. He saw the whole thing again. Every horrible detail returned, more dreadful than before. From the dark cavern of the past rose the image of his sin, terrible and wrapped in scarlet.

As I put my hand through the valve, carrying a cup of water for the old cat, my shirtsleeves caught in the loop supporting the basket and instantly dislodged it from the bottom. Had the whole thing actually dissolved into thin air, it could not have disappeared from view more suddenly or completely. I am certain that less than a tenth of a second passed between the basket coming loose and its utter disappearance, together with everything inside it. My good wishes accompanied it down to earth, but naturally I had no hope that either the cat or her kittens would survive to tell the story of their misfortune.

“At six o’clock, I noticed that a large part of the earth visible to the east was covered in deep shadow. This continued spreading very rapidly until, at five minutes to seven, the entire surface within my view lay wrapped in the darkness of night. Yet a considerable time passed before the setting sun’s rays stopped lighting the balloon. Although I had, of course, fully expected this, it still gave me tremendous pleasure. Clearly, in the morning I would see the sun rise at least several hours before the citizens of Rotterdam, despite their position so much farther east. Thus, with each passing day, and in proportion to the height I reached, I would enjoy sunlight for longer and longer periods. I now decided to keep a journal of my journey, counting each day continuously from one to twenty-four hours, without regard to the intervals of darkness.

“At ten o’clock, feeling sleepy, I decided to lie down for the remainder of the night. But a difficulty now arose which, obvious though it may seem, had escaped my notice until that very moment. If I went to sleep as intended, how would the air in the chamber be refreshed while I slept? It would be impossible to go on breathing it for more than an hour at the very most. Even if that period could be stretched to an hour and a quarter, the consequences might be disastrous. Considering this predicament caused me considerable anxiety. You may find it hard to believe that, after all the dangers I had already endured, I should regard this problem so seriously that I abandoned hope of achieving my final purpose and eventually decided I would have to descend. But my hesitation lasted only a moment.

Then I recited to myself the whole beautiful passage describing Dante’s entrance into the earthly Paradise. I thought how wonderful it would be, while walking along those lovely banks, to see the chariot of light descend, bringing my long-lost father back to me. As I waited there, anticipating that moment, I imagined weaving a garland from the beautiful flowers growing around me and crowning myself with it in joy. I would sing ‘sul margine d’un rio,’ my father’s favourite song, and my voice, floating through the still air, would tell him, in whatever shaded retreat he waited for our reunion, that his daughter had arrived. By then the mark of suffering would have disappeared from my forehead, and I would lift my eyes fearlessly to his, which always shone with the gentle brightness of innocent love. Remembering the magical expression of those deep eyes, I wept—but softly, afraid my sobs might disturb the enchanted scene.

I was so completely absorbed in this vision that I walked on without watching my steps. Only when I actually bent to pick a flower for my wreath, on that barren plain where no flowers grew, did I wake from my daydream and discover that I had no idea where I was.

The sun had set, and the rosy colour it had left on the clouds as it descended had almost faded. Wind swept across the plain. I looked around but saw nothing to tell me my location; I was lost, and tried unsuccessfully to find my path. I continued wandering, while the gathering darkness blurred every trace that might have guided me. At last everything disappeared into the deep obscurity of a pitch-black night. I grew tired, and knew that my servant was spending the night in the neighbouring village, so no one would be alarmed by my absence. I also knew that in this desolate place I was safe from any intruder, and I decided to stay where I was until morning. Indeed, I was too exhausted to walk any farther. The air was cold, but I cared little for physical discomfort, and thought myself thoroughly accustomed to the weather after two years of solitude, during which no change of season had interrupted my constant wandering.

I lay on the grass in darkness untouched by even the faintest ray of light. There was no sound: the deep night had put the insects to sleep, and they were the only creatures living in this lonely place, where neither tree nor shrub offered shelter to anything else. A marvellous silence filled the air, soothing my senses while awakening my soul. My mind rushed from one image to another and seemed to embrace an eternity.
